# Rewriting ("refactoring") a CSCI 435 issue spec with ab-wm

Specs in this course are graded (requirements spec, peer-reviewed by a teammate before coding), and the
issues ab-wm inherits are often AI-drafted: "entirely vibecoded with likely no review". Their job is to
turn them into specs a teammate can review and they can implement in small commits. Claude's job is the
legwork — reading every linked issue, checking every claim against the code, laying out the choices —
while they make the calls and post everything themselves.

Read `references/user-profile.md` once per session (how they work, and why), and use
`references/course-formats.md` §1 for the issue format. `references/spec-examples.md` has two of their
settled issues (#58, #59): match that structure, tone and level of detail.

## Ground rules

- **Claude never writes to GitHub.** No issue edits, comments, labels, milestones or new issues — unless
  they grant one specific action, and then only that one ("I give you permission to edit it for just
  proofing; don't change or write sentences"). Even then, back up the current body first and check it
  hasn't changed since you read it. Everything else is a draft they paste.
- **Drafts live in `.specstory/`** (gitignored): `.specstory/issue-<N>-rewrite/issue-<N>-draft.md` is
  exactly what they paste; `notes.md` beside it is for them only (claims check, what changed and why,
  knock-on edits for other issues, a rough commit plan).
- **One question at a time**, as numbered questions with lettered options and a recommendation; they
  answer "1a" or "a". Give real pushback when you disagree. When they've asked for a draft, the
  question comes after the draft, not instead of it.
- **No implementation detail in the issue.** "issues should [not] detail implementation details, that is
  for the implementor, not the issue creator." File paths, functions and designs go in `notes.md`.
- **Design decisions are not written up front.** "decisions will come later as I implement them, since I
  don't even know what those decisions are." Their issues say: *Added per commit during implementation,
  as in #53 and #54.* (Teammates' issues may carry spec-time decisions; that's their call.)
- **Tech debt belongs to the PR, not the issue** — but note scope that's being deferred, because it may
  become a tech-debt point later.
- **Evidence for every claim** (`file:line`), and re-fetch live GitHub state before saying anything about
  it ("it has been closed already? check again").

## Where you are running

- **Claude Code in the repo:** use `gh issue view <N> --comments`, `gh api` for sub-issues and
  blocked-by links, and read the code locally.
- **claude.ai or anywhere without the repo:** fetch the public issue and files with the URLs in
  `references/working-without-the-repo.md`, or ask them to paste the issue. You can still do the whole
  workflow; say which code claims you couldn't verify.

## Current sprint: Sprint 3 (Nov 3–19, 2026)

Source: https://csci-435-se.github.io/sprint3/. Sprint 1 and 2 rules still apply unless that page
changes them. Where it disagrees with `references/course-formats.md` or the repo's
`.claude-students/COURSE-WORKFLOW.md` (which still described Sprint 2 on Nov 4), the sprint page wins.
Re-read it when something is unclear, because it may have changed since this was written.

What it changes for specs:

- **Specs are written and reviewed before coding.** The review is a teammate's comment on the issue,
  and it has to say what was checked. A bare "Looks good!" doesn't count. Writing the user's
  reviews of teammates' specs is the `csci435-spec-review` skill.
- **Every issue justifies its scope:** small or medium, plus one or two sentences on which components
  it touches and how much change to expect. The TA may reclassify scope that's clearly overstated.
  Only small and medium exist. CSCI 435 students need at least two medium issues, or the equivalent
  points.
- **The format depends on the kind of issue.** A feature keeps the user-story format. A bug, including
  a hardening fix of a defect, uses the bug format (observed and expected behaviour, steps to
  reproduce, other details). Other work, such as refactors, CI or test fixes, uses a short task
  format: the problem, the goal, acceptance criteria and other details. The course gives no headings
  for it, so use `## Problem`, `## Goal`, then the usual sections from Acceptance Criteria onwards.
- **The backlog starts with unfinished Sprint 2 issues.** One that's dropped needs a comment on the
  issue saying why. Every selected issue goes on the `Sprint 3` milestone.
- **The team feature.** The instructor or TA posts a larger feature (spanning Sprints 3 and 4) as an
  issue. The team splits it into sub-issues, each with an owner, its own spec and scope, linked as a
  sub-issue of the feature, and on the Sprint 3 milestone. They count toward the minimum.
- **Hardening issues** (optional: one of theirs may be one) make the existing system more reliable.
  Candidates come from the team's baseline test run, the Introduced and Encountered tech debt in their
  Sprint 1 and 2 PRs, known bugs, and the upstream tracker. The ACs must name the evidence the PR will
  carry:
  - a bug fix: a test that fails before the fix and passes after it;
  - a flaky test: the root cause, plus repeated runs before and after (20 for a unit test, 10 for an
    E2E test);
  - a broken or missing CI check: links to CI runs before and after;
  - failing tests in the baseline: pass and fail counts before and after, and the cause of each group.

  Regenerating snapshots, reformatting code, or silencing a check without fixing its cause counts as
  small at most.
- **ACs must give the expected values.** Each PR's Test Evidence table now cites where every expected
  value came from, and the AC is the usual source. An AC that leaves the observable result vague (which
  label, count, message or page) pushes the implementer toward taking the value from the code's output,
  which the course rejects. Make such ACs specific, or flag them in a review.

## The workflow

### 1. Read everything, change nothing

Read the issue, its comments, its parent, its sub-issues and siblings, and every blocked-by/blocking
link, plus labels, milestone and assignee. What comes next depends on what they asked for:

- **A review first** ("do a quick review … no obvious holes that change the prescribed implementation"):
  report only the holes that would change *the prescribed implementation, the ACs, or the blocking
  relationships*, then stop. Wording gets fixed during the rewrite; don't list it.
- **The rewrite itself** ("rewrite it in my style", "write a draft"): do steps 2–4 in this same reply,
  and hand back the draft. Don't hold it back for a question. When they asked this way on #56, the
  draft came in the first reply. Open choices go after the draft (step 3).

### 2. Check the claims against the code

For every factual claim the spec makes about the product (what a page shows, how a handler behaves,
which file owns something), build a table in `notes.md`:

| Claim | Holds? | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "`g c` goes where the Code tab links" | No | on a non-default branch the tab links to that branch (`templates/repo/header.tmpl:87`) |

Note any real bugs you find on the way. When the feature mirrors another product ("GitHub's `g`
shortcuts"), check that product's actual behaviour (GitHub docs) — their rule became "match GitHub,
nothing more fancy", because users can't discover invented behaviour. Ignore what Gitea upstream's
original issue wanted: "the target is not to match the original."

### 3. Settle scope, one question at a time

If they already asked for the draft, write it with your recommended option and put the question
after it: "The draft uses (b); say a or c and I'll swap the wording." Otherwise ask before drafting.

- What the issue covers, and what moves elsewhere. Too much for one issue → propose a split (step 5).
  Behaviour that really belongs to a sibling → point at the sibling rather than absorbing it ("But then
  that sounds like scope creep").
- Who the user story is for. One story per issue. For a foundation or refactor issue the persona is the
  next developer, plus one sentence on where end users get the value.
- Size it honestly, by the work, not the look: "is it not medium from work point of view, or only in
  appearance?" Use one points range per size across the sprint, and remember the course's per-student
  load (at least two medium issues or equivalent points). The size needs a written justification in
  the issue (see the Sprint 3 section), so base it on the components the work really touches.
- Prefer the least intrusive fix for cross-issue dependencies.

### 4. Draft the spec

Write `issue-<N>-draft.md` in the course format (course-formats §1), modelled on `spec-examples.md`:

- `> Blocked by #N, which adds …` at the top when it is.
- User Story, then a concrete User Scenario (who, where, what they do and see), with a small table when
  it lists several cases.
- ACs as `- [ ] ACn: Given …, when …, then …`, one observable pass/fail result each, at least three.
  Regression ACs say "as … does today". Name exact labels and locale strings when the UI text matters.
- Out of Scope as bullets, pointing at the sibling issue that covers each item ("…: Issue (#57)").
- Open Questions: "None", or the real ones.
- Design Decisions: the per-commit placeholder (see ground rules).
- Scope: `small (2 points)` / `medium (3 points)` — matching the `scope:` label — followed by one or
  two plain sentences on which parts of Gitea it touches and how much change to expect, e.g. "medium
  (3 points). Touches the repo header template and the shortcut registry; about three small changes
  plus tests." Name areas, not functions.
- Scope Change Reasoning when the rewrite changed scope (what moved, and to which new issue).
- AI Disclosure: "Used claude-code for the drafting of this issue, followed by my changes and proofing."
- Titles keep backticks around keys and code (`` `g` navigation shortcuts … ``).

Keep the language plain; the reader is a teammate reviewing a spec, not an implementer.

### 5. Split off a new issue when needed

Draft its body the same way (often for someone else: no assignee), with its parent (sub-issue of the
epic), its blocked-by links, and a note on what it took from the original. Update the original's Out of
Scope and Scope Change Reasoning to point at it. They create it on GitHub; then re-check numbers.

### 6. Knock-on edits to other issues

List the edits each sibling or parent issue needs, with line references, in `notes.md`. If they've
already edited some ("I have alraedy made edits … So tell me what I need to add"), give only the delta.
Leave issues that aren't theirs alone unless they say otherwise.

### 7. "check" — verify what they posted

After each of their edits, re-fetch the live issue and check: the body matches the agreed draft; no
`TODO` issue numbers or placeholders are left; titles keep their backticks; labels (`enhancement`,
`scope: small|medium`), milestone (`Sprint 3`), parent and blocked-by links are right (a team-feature
sub-issue is linked to the feature issue); the Scope line has its justification; any `Deferred` label is
removed if the issue is now in the sprint; a dropped Sprint 2 carryover has its "why dropped" comment; no
leftover draft comments; the AI Disclosure is filled in. Report only what's off.

### 8. After a teammate's spec review

Sort the points of their spec review ("Spec reviewed — …" or a review table) into real fixes, wrong
premises and nitpicks. Apply the real fixes to the draft in the user's voice (when they ask) and add to
the AI Disclosure: "Changes after the spec review were also made with claude-code." They write the reply
to the reviewer themselves ("Feedback noted and in." / "Changes in") — don't draft replies to reviewers
for them.

If the review on their issue doesn't say what was checked (a bare approval), point it out once: the
course doesn't count it, and coding is meant to wait for a real one. Whether to ask the reviewer for
more is their call.

### 9. Reviewing a teammate's spec

That's a separate job with its own graded format: use the `csci435-spec-review` skill.

## Reference files

- `references/user-profile.md` — who ab-wm is and how they like to work (read every session).
- `references/course-formats.md` — the issue format (§1) and the other course formats, as of Sprint 2.
  The Sprint 3 section above adds to it: scope justification, and task and hardening issues.
- `references/spec-examples.md` — their settled issues #58 and #59, as the model.
- `references/working-without-the-repo.md` — reading issues and code from claude.ai.

# Working with ab-wm

Who they are and how they like to work, distilled from every session of the CSCI 435 project
(Sept–Oct 2026). Quotes are theirs. Read this once at the start of a session; it saves them from
"start[ing] with the same spiel" every time.

## Contents
1. Who they are
2. How to talk to them
3. Decisions and pushback
4. Scope and design instincts
5. Git, GitHub and drafts
6. Testing and verification
7. Writing that gets posted or graded
8. Reviews: theirs of others, others' of theirs
9. Tokens and time
10. What frustrates them

## 1. Who they are

- A student (GitHub `ab-wm`, git `abhoot`) on a 5-person team building features in a fork of Gitea
  for CSCI 435. The fork "will probably never get merged, but for the sake of the assignment" they
  still want Gitea's own standards, "as if we were the main devs of the project".
- Comfortable with TypeScript, React and CSS. New to Go, Go templates and Vue ("I am a beginner
  after all"). Anchor explanations in TS/React and say where the analogy breaks (in Gitea the HTML is
  rendered by Go and *found* by the TypeScript; the DOM is the state).
- The real goal is learning to navigate a large codebase: "I don't want you to simply give me the
  answer … I want to understand how to even navigate software like this." They want to understand
  every change they land.
- Messages are terse, lowercase, typo-heavy, often amended a minute later in parentheses
  ("(no, 600 after this run)"). Read for intent; a stray refused tool call or interrupt is often an
  accident ("oops, accidentally refused comand") — ask rather than treat it as a no.
- They work late at night, on a limited student token plan, against sprint deadlines.

## 2. How to talk to them

- **One thing at a time.** "lets go one by one", "One at a time.", "no need to be *that* pedantic."
  One decision or one step per reply; finish it, report it, stop.
- **Lay out before doing** when a step isn't already agreed: "explain commit 4 before making
  changes", "lay it out". Once a plan or decision covers it, just do it and present the result.
- **Start from what they can see.** "get me to the page where the change is going to occur, and then
  work backwards." Say which layer you're in and why; a tiny ASCII diagram helps when they're lost
  ("sorry, you lost me … forget about the tests, what *are* we changing here, and for what purpose").
- **Short and plain.** Define jargon you use ("Explain 'tangled with the popups'"). Answer the simple
  question asked ("i mean, I just want to switch it?"). Keep text short when they'll rewrite it anyway.
- **Concrete over abstract.** When unsure what you mean they ask ("twice in html or twice on display,
  like two bells over each other"); pre-empt by being specific.
- They reply to numbered lists point by point ("1. Im not doing that … 2. fixed …"); number your items.
- When they ask "is that it?", give a clear list of what's left, and whose job each item is.

## 3. Decisions and pushback

- **They decide.** "I am the one who needs to make decisions. Any ambiguity should be pased by me."
- **Format:** numbered questions with lettered options, a recommendation and its reason; they answer
  "1a, 3c" or just "a". For each choice, they also say whether it deserves a written decision
  ("quality vs quantity") — ask when it's unclear.
- **Real pushback, not agreement.** "no pushback? Huh." / "I felt like you just went along with me."
  / "don't just go along with me." Give your honest view with evidence even when it disagrees.
- **Check before conceding.** When they cite a source ("course requirements: <link>"), read it before
  answering — "Did you even check the link?" Then say which part supports them and which doesn't, and
  respect their call.
- **Expect "why".** "but why, … why put a string in the package instead of a file", "what is the point
  of the first check?" Be ready to justify each choice, and confirm your own claims ("'seems to serve
  no purpose' Confirm that").
- **Re-check live state** instead of trusting an earlier read: "it has been closed already? check
  again." They also re-check thin results: "this was an awfully short medium issue. Are you sure you
  are not missing anything?"

## 4. Scope and design instincts

- **Gitea precedent first.** "is there a precendent that backs that?", "how does the rest of gitea
  handle this", "nah, let it be if there is precedent". Find the existing pattern before proposing one.
- **Reuse over new.** Existing validators, existing widgets (the `#` issue picker), existing locale
  strings ("ditch the message element, so the locale … does not need to change").
- **One general mechanism over many per-page edits**, designed so adding a case later needs no new
  front-end code.
- **No hacks.** "isnt the dispatch a random event a bit of a dirty fix?" Change a function signature
  when the design calls for it rather than contorting around it; mark backwards-compatibility shims
  with a comment.
- **Least intrusive correct fix.** "what is the least intrusive way to do this properly".
- **Scope discipline.** Out-of-scope stays out, existing FIXMEs included; unrelated pre-existing
  breakage is left out of their PR ("Mentioning it would make it seem it was broken due to this
  work"). Extra behaviour becomes a new issue, possibly for someone else; a parent issue that asked for
  too much gets a scope-change note. Don't drift: "I don't want to spend hours on this."
- **UI/UX:** they defer to Gitea's look ("I know nothing about UI/UX design, follow how the precedent
  does it") but notice when something "aint quite there". A user must always be able to tell why
  something is blocked.
- **Conventions over reviewer suggestions** that would change them: "Im not doing that. That would be
  a convention change."

## 5. Git, GitHub and drafts

- **Never commit for them.** "You CANNOT commit on my behalf, ever." / "YOU ARE NOT PERMITTED TO
  COMMIT ON MY BEHALF, although you can provide a suggestion." Stage, draft the message, stop; they say
  "committed" / "go ahead". Write the suggested message into `.git/MERGE_MSG` and
  `.specstory/commit-msg.txt` when staging ("also stage them with the suggested … message").
- **Small commits, one concern each.** "Small changes every commit." A distinct concern gets its own
  commit and often its own decision. Cleanup or review fixes may be bundled when they say so. Docs
  don't need their own commit per page ("Commits … should be used to protect against breaking changes,
  so docs aint one of them").
- **Their commit messages are theirs**, brief by choice. Mention a missing `(#N)` or a typo once; they
  may simply explain it in review instead of rewriting ("7. explanation.").
- **No history rewriting once pushed.** "do not force anything, per repo req." Unpushed local commits
  can be reworded; they run it.
- **GitHub is read-only for Claude.** "DO NOT WRITE TO GH, read only." / "I don't permit you to change
  my stuff on github." No issues, PRs, comments, labels or CI reruns — unless they grant one specific
  action, and then only that action ("I give you permission to edit it for just proofing; don't change
  or write sentences"). One grant is not standing permission.
- **Drafts live in `.specstory/`** (gitignored). When GitHub text needs changing, edit the matching
  local draft so they can paste it whole ("why not edit the pr description I have already here"),
  after diffing it against the live GitHub text.
- **They keep their own copies** (`.specstory/decisions.md`, `.specstory/tech-debt.md`, reused per
  issue) "so they do not come in between of your edits". Look for them with `ls -lt .specstory/` and
  apply every fix there too, keeping their wording; plain typos may be fixed ("can fix typos, idc").
  They empty their decisions file after posting — that's not lost work.
- **Blocked by an unmerged PR?** They rehearse the whole implementation in a gitignored sandbox
  worktree "as if it was going to be commited", then replay it with `cherry-pick -n`, folding review
  fixes into the commits they fix.

## 6. Testing and verification

- **A test per acceptance criterion**, with an AC → test mapping written down ("Can you give me a list
  for the mapping between AC and test?"). "only 1 test for all of this?" is a complaint.
- **Tests check real behaviour**, not stored values. Unit tests for isolated logic, Playwright for
  wiring; explain *why* each kind in the PR (graded: "test strategy explained in PR").
- **Prove the tests can fail** (mutation checks) and report them.
- **They test visually too** — tell them exactly where in the UI to look. Claude may use a headless
  browser against their `make watch` instance; Firefox is available, LibreWolf is the "websites tend to
  break" browser, and local WebKit/GTK quirks don't matter.
- **Verify before the final commits and before the PR**, and after many back-and-forths ("some obvious
  facts might have slipped through"). When fixing several findings: tests first, then docs.
- **Use specific tools**, not repo-wide sweeps ("it does not need to be a repo wide make fmt"). Use
  make targets "for my own reference".
- Keep a local test bed, but delete leftover demo repos and throwaway test users afterwards.
- CI is theirs to run and rerun; when it fails, explain the cause (flake, teammate's code, or ours)
  before they push anything.

## 7. Writing that gets posted or graded

- **Plain language, no implementation detail.** "Implementation details are useless; you can't read
  code like you can't read maths." Decisions explain the decision, not the implementation ("they should
  not be that implementation heavy").
- **Their voice wins.** They often write or edit the draft, then ask "Have a look … Refine it more" /
  "keep my language, but fix the other problems." Fix facts and form; don't rewrite their sentences.
- **Own words for reflective/graded answers** (diagram Q&A, check-ins): give facts as bullets; they
  deliberately write lighter ("it does not truly represent what I understand"); edit for form and
  accuracy only.
- **PRs follow their previous PRs plus the course rules**: combined "What changed and why" heading
  ("it flows better since you can match the why with the what"), a test strategy about the *why* ("too
  heavy on the what instead of the why"), an Implementation Note instead of screenshots when nothing
  visible changed, real before/after screenshots when something did (never a demo repo; they upload
  images, Claude lays out the markdown).
- **No false claims.** Every statement in a PR or decision must match the code and the tests; numbers
  come from actual runs. Reviewers keep catching overstated claims.
- **Tech debt only when real**: "don't just shoehorn a tech-dept in, but when it is applicable."
- **AI disclosure:** they write and update the issue's AI Assistance comment and put log links in
  themselves; draft it only when asked. Don't remind them about `specstory sync` (it doesn't work in
  their setup). Never write their replies to reviewers on their own issue/PR (course policy) — proofread
  form only when asked.

## 8. Reviews

**Reviewing a teammate's PR** (there is a separate `csci435-pr-review` skill for this): surface level —
"don't be *that* deep … This does not mean to overlook stuff, but this also does not mean to nitpick";
no workflows for it; check scope against the issue; draft in `.specstory`; report findings and never
offer to fix their code.

**Reviewing their own work before the PR:** a lean workflow (about 3 agents) that also emulates the
reviewers they actually get — CodeRabbit's configured checks and a teammate's AI-assisted rubric —
"(protect against reviews, saves time in the long run)".

**Responding to reviews of their PR:** sort the review into real fixes, wrong premises and taste; they
decide. Taste and admin nits "should not hold back a PR". They push back on CodeRabbit's
What/Why-headings and screenshot checks by pointing to earlier PRs. Real code findings get fixed (with a
test) and a brief reply.

## 9. Tokens and time

- Limited plan: "the plans we students have access to are limited in the number of Tokens." State the
  agent count and token estimate before any workflow; never a full multi-agent review ("Please, please,
  please, do not do a full review workflow"). Lean reviews of ~250k are acceptable; they'll say when
  they have more room.
- Near the limit: stop long runs and switch to the deliverable ("Lets get the PR description in").
  "Last run" means compile the findings and apply them, no new exploration.
- Accuracy matters, but "lets not dwadle too long over an issue."

## 10. What frustrates them

- Agreeing without checking; missing a requirement they then have to point out ("you are missing one
  of the requirements. Technical debt. Check the sprint 2 site again").
- Losing them in detail or doing several things at once.
- Wrong or useless output (nonsense screenshots, the wrong file, truncated rubric text).
- Hacky fixes; scope creep (theirs or a teammate's); nitpicks that slow things down.
- Vibe-coded specs and reviews with no thought behind them.
- Their own draft copies being overlooked.
- Having to repeat these instructions at the start of every session.

## Summary
Let maintainers declare that one pull request depends on another. Display those dependencies and optionally enforce their merge order, so dependent changes do not merge before the code they require.

## User story
As a maintainer reviewing related changes, I want Gitea to block a dependent pull request until its prerequisites merge so that unfinished dependencies do not break the target branch.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Authorized users can add and remove prerequisite pull requests within the same repository.
- [ ] Pull request pages show prerequisites, their status, and links to dependent pull requests.
- [ ] Self-dependencies and dependency cycles are rejected.
- [ ] A repository setting enables merge blocking for unresolved prerequisites.
- [ ] Closing a prerequisite without merging it does not satisfy the dependency.
- [ ] Web, API, and automatic merge paths enforce the same rule.
- [ ] Tests cover dependency changes, cycles, permissions, and merge enforcement.

## Rough scope
**Large.** At least one sprint for dependency management, UI, merge-path enforcement, and tests. Cross-repository dependencies, automatic rebasing, and merge queues are excluded.

## Source
Upstream [go-gitea/gitea#38231, Dependent pull requests](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/issues/38231). This proposal limits the first version to one repository.

Bug report: `## Observed Behavior`, `## Expected Behavior`, `## Steps to Reproduce`,
`## Additional Information`, `## Design Decision`.

Peer review (D2): a teammate comments `Spec reviewed — <notes>` before implementation starts. Apply
their notes to the body, reply briefly ("Feedback noted and in."), and answer anything you disagree
with.

## 2. Design decisions (D3, graded strictly)

Every issue needs at least one non-trivial decision naming at least two concrete alternatives.
Four fields, plain language (what was chosen and what it means for users and developers; few
identifiers, no test-harness internals):

```markdown
## Design Decisions - @ab-wm

### Decisions for Commit 1
#### Decision 1: <the choice, as a sentence>

**Decision:** <what was chosen>
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) <option>. (b) <option>.
**Rationale:** <why this one, and why each alternative lost — refer to them as (a), (b)>
**Consequences:** <what it makes easier, harder, or leaves for later>
```

Decisions are numbered across the whole issue and grouped by the commit that made them
(`### Decisions for Commits 4 and 7` when a later commit changed one). Older issues used
`# Design Decision for the <Nth> commit (<what it did>)` headings; match whatever the issue already uses.
A later correction goes under `#### Correction` beneath the decision instead of silently rewriting it.

## 3. Commits and branches

- Branch from an up-to-date main: `feat/issue-<N>-short-description` (or `fix/`, `chore/`,
  `refactor/`). One issue per branch.
- Conventional Commits, subject ending with the issue number: `feat(shortcut): add c to … (#59)`.
  `test` type for test-only changes, `docs(context)` for `.claude-students`, `chore(ai-log)` for logs.
- Trailer when AI helped: `Assisted-by: Claude Code:claude-opus-5-5`. Never `Co-Authored-By` or
  `Signed-off-by`.
- The human makes every commit (see the user profile). Never amend, rebase or force-push anything
  already pushed; after review starts, new commits only, and merge main in rather than rebasing.

Grading: correctness against the ACs 6, test strategy with explanation 5, description quality
incl. Tech Debt 4, CI or manual verification 3, review rubric posted 2.

| AC | What the tests check |
| --- | --- |
| AC1 | ... |

- CI runs on the PR; per the course rules, it must pass before merging.
- `make test-frontend`: <N> tests pass, including the <k> new ones.
- `make lint-js`, `make lint-templates` ... pass.
- The <N> Playwright tests in `<file>` pass locally on Chromium and Firefox; each new one runs in under <t> s.

## Design

## Tech Debt
**Introduced:**
- <real items only, or "None.">

Both fields required; `None.` is valid. Only real items: a shortcut actually taken, or existing debt

## 7. Code review rubric (reviewing a teammate's PR)

Post as a PR comment as well as the GitHub review:

```markdown
### Code Review — @ab-wm

**Checked:** <what you ran or tried>

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correctness — implements issue requirements | | |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | | |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | | |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | | |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | | |
| Overall — merge as-is? | | |
```

ab-wm's review style: triage first (chores, docs, check-ins, log-only PRs get a one-line approval);
scores start at 10 and drop only for a concrete gap; optional nits are cut (at most one survives, in
its own "Strictly optional" section); one-sentence notes with `file:line` for code findings; they
write the testing paragraph themselves (leave a placeholder); end with `### AI-Log` saying the review
was AI-drafted then edited and pointing to the issue that holds the log. Report findings and stop —
never offer to fix a teammate's PR.

## Issue #58 — `g` navigation shortcuts for repository tabs and notifications

Labels: enhancement, scope: medium. Milestone: Sprint 2.

````markdown
> Blocked by #56, which adds the shortcut registry these shortcuts are built on.

## User Story

As a Gitea user who knows GitHub's keyboard shortcuts, I want the same two-key `g` shortcuts to perform the same behavior, taking me to a repository's code, issues, pull requests, actions and wiki, and to my notifications, so that I can move around without reaching for the mouse.

## User Scenario
A reviewer is reading a file on a feature branch. They press `g` then `i` and land on the repository's issue list, then `g` then `p` for the pull request list. Pressing `g` then `c` takes them back to the repository's front page on its default branch, the same as on GitHub. From anywhere in Gitea, while signed in, `g` then `n` opens their notifications.

A shortcut only works when its tab is shown. On a repository with the wiki turned off, or one that uses an external wiki, pressing `g` then `w` does nothing at all: no navigation, no error.

| Keys | Goes to | Works when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `g c` | The repository's front page, default branch | The Code tab is shown |
| `g i` | Issues | Gitea's own issue tracker is shown |
| `g p` | Pull requests | The Pull requests tab is shown |
| `g a` | Actions | The Actions tab is shown |
| `g w` | Wiki | Gitea's own wiki is shown |
| `g n` | Notifications | The user is signed in (any page) |

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a page inside a repository, when the user presses `g` then `i`, `p`, `a` or `w`, then the browser goes to that repository's Issues, Pull requests, Actions or Wiki tab.
- [ ] AC2: Given a page inside a repository while browsing a branch other than the default, when the user presses `g` then `c`, then the browser goes to the repository's front page on its default branch, even though the Code tab itself links to the branch being browsed.
- [ ] AC3: Given a tab that is not shown (its unit is disabled, the user cannot read it, or it is Actions on an empty repository), when the user presses its shortcut, then nothing happens and the page does not navigate.
- [ ] AC4: Given a repository that uses an external issue tracker or an external wiki, when the user presses `g i` or `g w`, then nothing happens and the browser never leaves Gitea.
- [ ] AC5: Given a narrow window where some tabs have moved into the tab bar's "more" menu, when the user presses one of their shortcuts, then it still works.
- [ ] AC6: Given any page while signed in, when the user presses `g` then `n`, then the browser goes to the notifications page; when signed out, nothing happens.
- [ ] AC7: Given a page outside any repository, when the user presses a repository shortcut such as `g i`, then nothing happens.
- [ ] AC8: Given the shortcuts on a page, when they are listed, then each repository shortcut is described by its tab's translated name (for example "Issues", without the open count) and is in the repository section, and `g n` is "Notifications" in the site-wide section.

## Out of Scope
- GitHub shortcuts for tabs Gitea does not have: Discussions (`g g`) and Security (`g s`).
- Shortcuts for tabs GitHub has no shortcut for: Releases, Projects, Packages, Activity and Settings.
- Other site-wide shortcuts, such as GitHub's `s` or `/` to focus the top search bar.
- Shortcuts that act on the current page instead of navigating, such as closing an issue or assigning labels.
- Showing the shortcuts to the user: Issue (#57)
- Changing what the tab bar shows or where its tabs link.

## Open Questions
None

## Design Decisions
Added per commit during implementation, as in #53 and #54. Noted below this issue as a comment (for brevity's sake).

## Scope
medium (3 points)

## AI Disclosure
Used claude-code for the drafting of this issue, followed by my changes and proofing. Changes after the spec review were also made with claude-code.

## Issue #59 — GitHub's `c` shortcuts for the issue and pull request lists and the pull request commit picker

Labels: enhancement, scope: small. Milestone: Sprint 2.

````markdown
> Blocked by #56, which adds the shortcut registry this shortcut is built on. AC5 also relies on #56's AC4: when `c` is the second key of `g c` (#58), it does not run this shortcut.

## User Story

As a Gitea user who knows GitHub's keyboard shortcuts, I want `c` to do what it does on GitHub, starting a new issue or pull request from the list and opening the commit picker on a pull request's changed files, so that I can start new work or narrow a review without reaching for the mouse.

## User Scenario
A maintainer working on a repository's issue list presses `c` and lands on the new issue page, or on the template chooser when the repository has issue templates, exactly as if they had clicked "New Issue". On the pull request list, `c` opens the new pull request page in the same way.

Later, reviewing a pull request's "Files changed" tab, they press `c`. The commit picker opens with its first entry, "Show all changes", focused; the arrow keys move through the commits and Escape closes it, as they do after clicking it. On an archived repository, where there is nothing to create, `c` on the lists does nothing.

| Page | `c` does | Works when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Issue list | Same as clicking "New Issue" | The "New Issue" button is shown |
| Pull request list | Same as clicking "New Pull Request" | The "New Pull Request" button is shown and enabled |
| A pull request's "Files changed" tab | Opens the commit picker | Always on that tab |

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a repository's issue list, when the user presses `c`, then the browser goes where the "New Issue" button leads: the new issue page, or the template chooser when the repository has issue templates.
- [ ] AC2: Given a repository's pull request list, when the user presses `c`, then the browser goes where the "New Pull Request" button leads.
- [ ] AC3: Given a list whose create button is missing or disabled (for example an archived repository, whose pull request list shows "Compare commits" instead), when the user presses `c`, then nothing happens.
- [ ] AC4: Given a pull request's "Files changed" tab, when the user presses `c`, then the commit picker opens with focus on its first entry, "Show all commits", and the arrow keys and Escape work as they do after clicking it.
- [ ] AC5: Given any other page, such as an issue's own page or the compare page, when the user presses `c`, then nothing happens.
- [ ] AC6: Given a page where `c` works, when the shortcuts are listed, then `c` is described by the translated label of what it opens ("New Issue", "New Pull Request" or "Filter by commit"), and is in the issue section on the lists and the pull request section on the "Files changed" tab.

## Out of Scope
- `r` related shortcuts: Issue (#95)
- `c` on other lists: milestone pages, and the site-wide or organisation Issues and Pull requests pages, as it is further scope than matching shortcut behaviors.
- GitHub's other list shortcuts (`u`, `l`, `m`, `a`, `o` and `Ctrl`/`Cmd`+`/`).
- Changing the create buttons or the commit picker themselves.
- Showing the shortcuts to the user: Issue (#57)

## Open Questions
None

## Design Decisions
Added per commit during implementation, as in #53 and #54. Noted below.

## Scope
small (2 points)

## Scope Change Reasoning
A significant portion of the issue was rewritten to better suit the task of matching Github's shortcuts and their behaviors. Since many of the previous behaviors were now out of scope, or belonged to another shortcut, a new Issue (#95) was created to implement `r` based shortcuts.

Course rules, not upstream Gitea ones. Source: the course site <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>

- **Carries forward:** anything the Sprint 3 page doesn't change comes from the Sprint 2 and

- **Start early:** record the test baseline at the Sprint 2 tag (see D8), and get the mutation tool

### Graded strictly this sprint

The Sprint 3 page lists these as the rules that cost the most points. Details are in the sections

1. No merge without a teammate's approval on the PR's **latest commit** (Reviews, below).

3. Every code PR has `Closes #<N>`, and both the issue and the PR are on the `Sprint 3` milestone.
4. Real AI logs, linked from the issue (D5).
5. A Test Evidence table in every PR, with expected values not copied from the code's output
   (Pull request format).
6. Mutation testing with a tool, with before and after reports committed (Mutation testing (D6)).
7. The team introduces no new test failures. A skipped test or a disabled CI check needs a linked
   issue and a reason in a code comment (D8).
8. A sprint report that renders on GitHub and uses the Sprint 3 sections (D8).

To pick up new work on `main` for a branch that already exists, **merge, don't rebase**. Rebasing

git merge origin/main
```

Do this before opening the PR and again if `main` moves while it is in review. A merge pushed after
approval needs a new approval (see Reviews). Never merge another feature branch into yours.

### After merge: clean up

A PR is merged with a merge commit once its latest commit is approved, every review comment is
addressed and CI passes. Then:

```bash

git branch -d feat/issue-<N>-short-description               # local branch
git push origin --delete feat/issue-<N>-short-description    # or GitHub's "Delete branch" button
git fetch --prune                                            # drop stale remote-tracking refs
```

## Issue format: feature (user story)

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user-story.yaml`. The user story must meet INVEST: Independent,
Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

```markdown
## User Story
As a <role>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>.

## User Scenario
<A short concrete walk-through: who, where in the UI, what they do, what they see.>

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given <state>, when <action>, then <observable result>.
- [ ] AC2: ...
- [ ] AC3: ...            (at least 3; each has a clear pass/fail result)

## Out of Scope
- <What this issue deliberately does not do.>

## Open Questions
- <Unresolved questions, or "None".>

## Design Decision
**Decision:** <what was chosen>
**Alternatives Considered:** <at least two concrete options, and why each lost>
**Rationale:** <why this one>
**Consequences:** <trade-offs, follow-up work, what it makes harder>

## Scope
small | medium | large, and matching `scope:` label
<One or two sentences on why: the components it touches and how much change you expect.>
```

## Issue format: bug report

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug-report.yaml`. Also used by hardening issues that fix a
defect.

```markdown
## Observed Behavior
## Expected Behavior
## Steps to Reproduce
1. ...
## Additional Information
<Version or commit, browser/OS, logs, screenshots.>
## Design Decision
<Same four fields as above: Decision, Alternatives Considered, Rationale, Consequences.>
## Scope
<Same as above: size, label and one or two sentences on why.>
```

## Issue format: hardening task

No GitHub template; write it in a blank issue. Used by hardening issues that don't fix a defect,
such as a flaky test or a broken CI check (Sprint 3, D2).

```markdown
## Problem
<What is unreliable now, and how you know: failing test names, run counts, CI run links.>
## Goal
<What "fixed" means.>
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: ...
## Evidence of Fix
<Which evidence from the table below the fix will show.>
## Design Decision
<Same four fields as above.>
## Scope
<Same as above: size, label and one or two sentences on why.>
```

### Hardening issues

Work that makes the existing system more reliable rather than adding a feature. Good sources: the
D8 baseline run (failing or flaky tests, broken CI checks on `main`); the "Introduced" and
"Encountered" Tech Debt fields of Sprint 1 and Sprint 2 PRs; bugs found in reviews or after
merging; and the upstream issue tracker for the parts of Gitea the team works on. It is scoped like
any other issue and must include evidence that the problem is fixed:

| Kind | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Bug fix | A test that fails before the fix and passes after |
| Flaky test | The root cause, and repeated runs before and after the fix (e.g. 20 for a unit test, 10 for E2E) |
| Broken or missing CI check | Links to CI runs before and after the fix |
| Failing tests in the baseline | Pass/fail counts before and after, and the cause of each group of failures |

The site doesn't say where the evidence goes: plan it in the issue (Evidence of Fix, or Additional
Information for a bug), then post the results on the issue and in the PR's Test Evidence once the
fix is in. Regenerating snapshots, reformatting code, or silencing a check without fixing its cause
counts as small at most.

### Design Decision and spec review

- **Design Decision (D3):** fill it in once you've picked an approach, before opening the PR. Put
  a second decision under another `### Decision 2` heading. If a PR changes the decision, update
  the issue body.
- **Spec review (D2):** before coding starts, a teammate posts a review comment **on the issue**.
  Start it with `Spec reviewed` so it is easy to find. The layout is the reviewer's choice, but the
  comment must say what was checked:
  1. each acceptance criterion: clear and testable, naming any that aren't;
  2. the cases considered (e.g. empty input, errors, permissions) and whether the ACs cover them;
  3. whether the scope fits the stated size;

  and end with an approval, or the problems for the author to fix in the spec. `Looks good!` with
  nothing about what was checked does not count. An optional layout:

  ```markdown
  Spec reviewed — @reviewer-username

  **Acceptance criteria:** <clear and testable? which aren't, and why>
  **Cases considered:** <which cases, and whether the ACs cover them>
  **Scope:** <does it fit the stated size?>
  **Verdict:** Approved | Changes needed: <list>
  ```

## Pull request format

Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.
`fix(issues): keep label filter after search`. Description sections:

1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge. Every code PR links its issue, and
   the PR goes on the `Sprint 3` milestone too.
2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
4. **Test Evidence:** required from Sprint 3. It replaces the old "How it was tested" section.
   Every behaviour change still needs a new or updated test.

   ```markdown
   ## Test Evidence

   | Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | AC1: ... | ... | ... | ... |

   **Not tested automatically, and why:** [...]

   **AI-written tests:** [Which tests were written or modified by AI, and how you checked that their expected values are correct. If none, write "None."]
   ```

   - **One row per acceptance criterion** from the issue; for a bug report, the Expected Behavior.
     A PR that changes no product behaviour (e.g. a CI change) writes `N/A` and why.
   - **Test(s):** the test name, plus the file if not obvious. For a manual check, write `Manual:`
     followed by the steps and what you saw. An AC tested both ways lists both in the same row.
   - **Level:** `unit`, `integration`, `E2E` or `manual`.
   - **Source of expected value:** `AC`, `issue discussion`, `docs`, `upstream behavior`, or
     `other` (explain). **Never the current output of your own code:** a test whose expected value
     was copied from what the code returns cannot detect that the code is wrong.
   - **Not tested automatically, and why:** only for ACs checked manually only.
   - AI may draft this section; the author checks that it is accurate.

5. **CI / manual verification:** CI status. If CI doesn't run your tests, the commands you ran and
   a summary of the results (passed, failed, skipped).
6. **Design:** one line pointing at the Design Decision in the issue, or a note on how it changed.
7. **Tech Debt:** required from Sprint 2. Both fields are required, and `None.` is a valid answer:

   ```markdown
   ## Tech Debt

   **Introduced:** <shortcuts, workarounds or design compromises this PR makes, and why>

   **Encountered:** <tech debt that was already there and that you ran into, and how you handled it>
   ```

8. **AI assistance:** format in `AI-ASSISTANCE.md` §2, with **no log link**.

Per-PR grading (20 points): correctness against the acceptance criteria 6; tests written or updated
appropriately, with the Test Evidence section complete, every AC covered and expected values
justified 6; description explains what and why, Tech Debt section present, issue linked 3; CI passes
or manual verification documented 3; reviewed with the rubric (including the test evidence row),
reviewer comment posted, merged only after an approval on the latest commit 2.

## Code review rubric

The reviewer posts this as a **PR comment**, as well as the GitHub review itself. A copy-paste copy
is in `.github/code-review-rubric.md`, so keep the two in sync. Pull the branch and test it when you
can, say what you checked, and mark each point as required or optional
(`docs/community-governance.md`). Score each row against the issue's acceptance criteria. Anything

## Issue Body

The author proposes letting a pull request declare dependencies on other pull requests, in the same repository or across repositories. Examples include a Gitea PR that adds API changes and a follow-up PR that uses them, or a library release that an application update depends on. The proposal would show dependencies, reverse dependencies, and their status in the UI. It also suggests an optional repository setting that blocks merging while dependencies are unresolved. The author notes this could support stacked PR workflows and is useful for package maintenance, coordinated releases, and multi-repository projects.

Maintainer 6543 wrote that a PR blocked by something it relies on should stay blocked, even if the dependency is a closed, unmerged PR. The page doesn't show that as a formal change to merge blocking.

func (err ErrUnknownDependencyType) Unwrap() error {
	return util.ErrInvalidArgument
}

// IssueDependency represents an issue dependency
type IssueDependency struct {
	ID           int64              `xorm:"pk autoincr"`
	UserID       int64              `xorm:"NOT NULL"`
	IssueID      int64              `xorm:"UNIQUE(issue_dependency) NOT NULL"`
	DependencyID int64              `xorm:"UNIQUE(issue_dependency) NOT NULL"`
	CreatedUnix  timeutil.TimeStamp `xorm:"created"`
	UpdatedUnix  timeutil.TimeStamp `xorm:"updated"`
}

func init() {
	db.RegisterModel(new(IssueDependency))
}

// DependencyType Defines Dependency Type Constants
type DependencyType int

// Define Dependency Types
const (
	DependencyTypeBlockedBy DependencyType = iota
	DependencyTypeBlocking
)

// CreateIssueDependency creates a new dependency for an issue
func CreateIssueDependency(ctx context.Context, user *user_model.User, issue, dep *Issue) error {
	return db.WithTx(ctx, func(ctx context.Context) error {
		// Check if it already exists
		exists, err := issueDepExists(ctx, issue.ID, dep.ID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if exists {
			return ErrDependencyExists{issue.ID, dep.ID}
		}
		// And if it would be circular
		circular, err := issueDepExists(ctx, dep.ID, issue.ID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if circular {
			return ErrCircularDependency{issue.ID, dep.ID}
		}

		if err := db.Insert(ctx, &IssueDependency{
			UserID:       user.ID,
			IssueID:      issue.ID,
			DependencyID: dep.ID,
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Add comment referencing the new dependency
		return createIssueDependencyComment(ctx, user, issue, dep, true)
	})
}

// RemoveIssueDependency removes a dependency from an issue
func RemoveIssueDependency(ctx context.Context, user *user_model.User, issue, dep *Issue, depType DependencyType) (err error) {
	return db.WithTx(ctx, func(ctx context.Context) error {
		var issueDepToDelete IssueDependency

		switch depType {
		case DependencyTypeBlockedBy:
			issueDepToDelete = IssueDependency{IssueID: issue.ID, DependencyID: dep.ID}
		case DependencyTypeBlocking:
			issueDepToDelete = IssueDependency{IssueID: dep.ID, DependencyID: issue.ID}
		default:
			return ErrUnknownDependencyType{depType}
		}

		affected, err := db.GetEngine(ctx).Delete(&issueDepToDelete)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// If we deleted nothing, the dependency did not exist
		if affected <= 0 {
			return ErrDependencyNotExists{issue.ID, dep.ID}
		}

		// Add comment referencing the removed dependency
		return createIssueDependencyComment(ctx, user, issue, dep, false)
	})
}

// Check if the dependency already exists
func issueDepExists(ctx context.Context, issueID, depID int64) (bool, error) {
	return db.GetEngine(ctx).Where("(issue_id = ? AND dependency_id = ?)", issueID, depID).Exist(&IssueDependency{})
}

// IssueNoDependenciesLeft checks if issue can be closed
func IssueNoDependenciesLeft(ctx context.Context, issue *Issue) (bool, error) {
	exists, err := db.GetEngine(ctx).
		Table("issue_dependency").
		Select("issue.*").
		Join("INNER", "issue", "issue.id = issue_dependency.dependency_id").
		Where("issue_dependency.issue_id = ?", issue.ID).
		And("issue.is_closed = ?", "0").
		Exist(&Issue{})

	return !exists, err
}

func markPullRequestStatusAsChecking(ctx context.Context, pr *issues_model.PullRequest) bool {
	pr.Status = issues_model.PullRequestStatusChecking
	_, err := pr.UpdateColsIfNotMerged(ctx, "status")
	if err != nil {
		log.Error("UpdateColsIfNotMerged failed, pr: %-v, err: %v", pr, err)
		return false
	}
	pr, err = issues_model.GetPullRequestByID(ctx, pr.ID)
	if err != nil {
				AddPullRequestToCheckQueue(pr.ID) // the queue is a unique queue and won't add the same task again
				return nil
			})
		}
	}
}

// CheckPullMergeable check if the pull mergeable based on all conditions (branch protection, merge options, ...)
// mergeStyle tailors the "require signed commits" prechecks:
//   - fast-forward-only: no Gitea commit is produced, so Gitea's merge-signing check is skipped;
//     only the user's head commits are verified.
//   - merge: both the head commits must be verified and Gitea must sign the merge commit.
//   - rebase, rebase-merge, squash: Gitea rewrites the commits and signs each, so only Gitea's
//     signing ability is checked.
func CheckPullMergeable(stdCtx context.Context, doer *user_model.User, perm *access_model.Permission, pr *issues_model.PullRequest, mergeCheckType MergeCheckType, mergeStyle repo_model.MergeStyle, forceMerge bool) error {

		if pr.HasMerged {
			return ErrHasMerged
		}

		if err := pr.LoadIssue(ctx); err != nil {

			return ErrIsClosed
		}

			log.Error("Error whilst checking if %-v is allowed to merge %-v: %v", doer, pr, err)
			return err
		} else if !allowedMerge {
			return ErrNoPermissionToMerge
		}

		if mergeCheckType == MergeCheckTypeManually {
			// if doer is doing "manually merge" (mark as merged manually), do not check anything
			return nil

	}

	issue, err := issues_model.GetIssueByIndex(ctx, repo.ID, form.Index)
	if err != nil {
		ctx.APIErrorAuto(err)
		return nil
	}
	issue.Repo = repo
	return issue
}

func getPermissionForRepo(ctx *context.APIContext, repo *repo_model.Repository) *access_model.Permission {
	if repo.ID == ctx.Repo.Repository.ID {
		return &ctx.Repo.Permission
	}

	perm, err := access_model.GetDoerRepoPermission(ctx, repo, ctx.Doer)
	if err != nil {
		ctx.APIErrorInternal(err)
		return nil
	}

	return &perm
}

func createIssueDependency(ctx *context.APIContext, target, dependency *issues_model.Issue, targetPerm, dependencyPerm access_model.Permission) {
	if target.Repo.IsArchived || !target.Repo.IsDependenciesEnabled(ctx) {
		// The target's repository doesn't have dependencies enabled
		ctx.APIErrorNotFound()
		return
	}

	if !targetPerm.CanWriteIssuesOrPulls(target.IsPull) {
		// We can't write to the target
		ctx.APIErrorNotFound()
		return
	}

	if !dependencyPerm.CanReadIssuesOrPulls(dependency.IsPull) {
		// We can't read the dependency
		ctx.APIErrorNotFound()
		return
	}

	err := issues_model.CreateIssueDependency(ctx, ctx.Doer, target, dependency)
	if err != nil {
		ctx.APIErrorInternal(err)
		return
	}
}

// handlePullRequestAutoMerge merge the pull request if all checks are successful
func handlePullRequestAutoMerge(pullID int64, sha string) {
	ctx, _, finished := process.GetManager().AddContext(graceful.GetManager().HammerContext(),
		fmt.Sprintf("Handle AutoMerge of PR[%d] with sha[%s]", pullID, sha))
	defer finished()

	pr, err := issues_model.GetPullRequestByID(ctx, pullID)
	if err != nil {
		log.Error("GetPullRequestByID[%d]: %v", pullID, err)
		return
	}

	// Check if there is a scheduled pr in the db
	exists, scheduledPRM, err := pull_model.GetScheduledMergeByPullID(ctx, pr.ID)
	if err != nil {
		log.Error("%-v GetScheduledMergeByPullID: %v", pr, err)
		return
	}
	if !exists {
		return
		return
	}

	perm, err := access_model.GetDoerRepoPermission(ctx, pr.BaseRepo, doer)
	if err != nil {
		log.Error("GetDoerRepoPermission %-v: %v", pr.BaseRepo, err)
		return
	}

	if err := pull_service.CheckPullMergeable(ctx, doer, &perm, pr, pull_service.MergeCheckTypeGeneral, scheduledPRM.MergeStyle, false); err != nil {
		if errors.Is(err, pull_service.ErrNotReadyToMerge) {
			log.Info("%-v was scheduled to automerge by an unauthorized user", pr)
			return
		}
		log.Error("%-v CheckPullMergeable: %v", pr, err)
		return
	}

	if err := pull_service.Merge(ctx, pr, doer, scheduledPRM.MergeStyle, "", scheduledPRM.Message, true); err != nil {
		log.Error("pull_service.Merge: %v", err)
		// FIXME: if merge failed, we should display some error message to the pull request page.
		// The resolution is add a new column on automerge table named `error_message` to store the error message and displayed
		// on the pull request page. But this should not be finished in a bug fix PR which will be backport to release branch.
		return
	}

```text
## Summary
In Gitea, a closed issue or pull request is simply "closed" — there's no way to tell whether it was fixed, rejected, a duplicate, or closed for some other reason. Maintainers end up writing "closing as duplicate of #12" in comments, and anyone browsing closed items later can't tell finished work from abandoned ideas.

This feature adds a **close reason** to issues and pull requests. The reason is chosen when closing, saved in the database, and shown on the issue/PR and in its timeline. Preset reasons cover the common cases, and an **Other** option lets the user type a custom reason. Items closed automatically (by a commit, a merged PR, a deleted branch, etc.) get a sensible reason too.

This helps maintainers triage faster, and helps contributors and project managers read a project's history accurately — for example, how much was actually completed versus declined.

## User story
As a repository maintainer, I want to choose why I'm closing an issue or pull request — from a list or by typing my own reason — so that anyone reading it later knows what happened without digging through comments.

## Proposed behavior

### Closing manually (web UI)
- The **Close** button on issues becomes a split button with a dropdown:
  - **Close as completed** (default)
  - **Close as not planned**
  - **Close as duplicate** — asks for the original issue number (e.g. `#12`)
  - **Close with other reason…** — shows a text box for a custom reason (required when chosen, max 255 characters)
- The **Close pull request** button gets the same dropdown **without "Completed"**, since a finished PR is *merged*, not closed. Options: **Not planned** (default), **Duplicate**, **Other…**. Merging stays a separate state and needs no reason.
- The **issue/PR list** bulk "Close" action offers the same reason choice (preset reasons only; one reason applied to all selected items).

### Saving and display
- A database migration adds to the `issue` table (which also stores PRs):
  - `close_reason` — `completed`, `not_planned`, `duplicate`, or `other`
  - `close_reason_text` — the custom text when the reason is `other`
  - `duplicate_of_id` — the original issue/PR when the reason is `duplicate`
- The same fields are stored on the close timeline comment, so every close/reopen in the history keeps its own reason.
- The timeline shows e.g. "closed this as not planned", "closed this as a duplicate of #12", or "closed this: *custom text*".
- Custom text is displayed as plain text (escaped, not rendered as Markdown/HTML).
- Closed items show a distinct icon/label per reason (e.g. "not planned" looks different from "completed").
- **Reopening** clears the current reason (the old reason stays visible in the timeline).
- Existing closed issues/PRs have no reason and display exactly as they do today.

### Automatic closing

| How it closes | Code path | Reason saved |
|---|---|---|
| Commit message keyword ("fixes #5") | `services/issue/commit.go` | Completed |
| Merged PR that references an issue | `services/pull/merge.go` | Completed (on the referenced issue) |
| PR auto-closed because its head branch was deleted | `services/pull/pull.go` (`AdjustPullsCausedByBranchDeleted`) | Not planned |
| PRs auto-closed because the repo's branches were removed | `services/pull/pull.go` (`CloseRepoBranchesPulls`) | Not planned |
| API call that closes without giving a reason | `routers/api/v1/repo/issue.go` | Completed (issues) / Not planned (PRs) |

### API
- Issue and pull request edit endpoints accept optional `close_reason` (`completed`, `not_planned`, `duplicate`, `other`), `close_reason_text`, and `duplicate_of` fields.
- Issue and PR JSON responses include `close_reason` and `close_reason_text` (similar to GitHub's `state_reason`).
- Invalid combinations are rejected with 422 (e.g. `other` with empty text, `duplicate` pointing at a nonexistent issue, `completed` on a PR).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A database migration adds the close-reason columns; existing issues and PRs are unaffected.
- [ ] Users can pick a preset reason or type a custom one when closing an issue or PR from its page.
- [ ] PRs do not offer "Completed"; merging still works without a reason.
- [ ] The bulk close action on issue/PR lists lets users pick a preset reason.
- [ ] "Duplicate" requires a valid issue/PR number in the same repository, and the timeline links to it.
- [ ] "Other" requires non-empty text (≤ 255 chars), which is saved and displayed escaped.
- [ ] Timeline and closed-item display show the reason; all new UI strings are in `locale_en-US.json`.
- [ ] Each automatic close path saves the reason listed in the table above.
- [ ] Reopening clears the current reason but keeps it in the timeline history.
- [ ] The API accepts, validates, and returns the close-reason fields for issues and PRs.
- [ ] Unit tests cover each reason, custom-text validation, each automatic path, and the migration.

## Implementation notes
- Every close goes through `issues_model.SetIssueAsClosed` (`models/issues/issue_update.go:51`), which currently only updates `is_closed` and `closed_unix`. The reason would be added there and passed down from `issue_service.CloseIssue` (`services/issue/status.go:17`) by each caller.
- Web routes: `routers/web/repo/issue_comment.go` (Close button) and `routers/web/repo/issue_list.go` (bulk close).
- Timeline close events are `CommentTypeClose` (`models/issues/comment.go:71`).
- Close button template: `templates/repo/issue/view_content.tmpl`.
- Possible follow-up: Gitea's GitHub migration test data already contains GitHub's `state_reason`, so a later issue could import close reasons when migrating from GitHub.

## Rough scope
**Large.** It touches every layer of Gitea — a database migration, the issue/PR model and services, several automatic-close paths, web UI in two places with custom-text input, the REST API, and tests — more than a single sprint of work.

## Source
Personal use and a feature gap compared to GitHub, which supports "Close as completed / not planned / duplicate". Our own team's tracker would benefit, since the current closed state can't tell finished work from declined work.

```markdown
## User Story

As a maintainer reviewing a pull request that builds on another one, I want it to stay blocked until the pull request it depends on is actually merged, so that closing the earlier one without merging it cannot let unfinished work into the target branch.

## User Scenario
Sam opens pull request #12, which uses an API that pull request #11 adds, and marks #12 as depending on #11 in the sidebar. A maintainer decides #11 needs a different approach and closes it without merging. Today, a closed #11 counts as done, so #12 can be merged and the target branch breaks.

With this change, #12 stays blocked. Pressing Merge shows an error saying why, the API refuses to merge it, and a scheduled "merge when checks succeed" does not go through. Once #11 is reopened and merged, #12 can be merged as usual. Dependencies on issues work as they do today: closing the issue is enough.

| #12 depends on | In state | Can #12 be merged? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An issue | Open | No, as today |
| An issue | Closed | Yes, as today |
| A pull request | Open | No, as today |
| A pull request | Merged | Yes, as today |
| A pull request | Closed without merging | **No** (today: yes) |

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given pull request B depends on pull request A, and A was closed without being merged, when a user with merge rights presses Merge on B, then B is not merged and the page shows "This pull request can't be merged until the pull requests it depends on are merged and the issues it depends on are closed."
- [ ] AC2: Given the same, when B is merged through the API, then the API answers 405 Method Not Allowed and B is not merged, as it does for the other reasons a pull request cannot be merged. Today it answers 500 Internal Server Error, for an open dependency too.
- [ ] AC3: Given the same, and B is scheduled to merge when its checks succeed, when B's checks succeed, then B is not merged and stays open.
- [ ] AC4: Given B depends on A, when A is merged, then B can be merged from the web and through the API, as today.
- [ ] AC5: Given B depends on an issue, when the issue is closed, then B can be merged, as today; while the issue is open, it cannot.
- [ ] AC6: Given B depends on A, and A was closed without being merged, when a user closes B, then B is closed, as today.
- [ ] AC7: Given a repository with "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" turned off in its settings, when a pull request whose dependencies are not resolved is merged, then it is merged, as closing an issue already ignores dependencies when the setting is off. Today the dependencies are hidden and cannot be removed, yet they still block the merge.

## Out of Scope
- Showing on the pull request page which dependencies block it, and whether each one is open, merged or closed: Issue (#<B>)
- Dependency loops of three or more, and the checks the API skips when a dependency is added: Issue (#<C>)
- Merging a scheduled pull request the moment its last dependency merges. As today, it is tried again when its checks or reviews next change.
- Letting administrators merge past a dependency. "Merge anyway" does not skip dependencies today, and that stays.
- "Mark as manually merged", which records a merge made outside Gitea and does not check dependencies, as today.
- A separate setting for merge blocking. The existing "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" setting decides (AC7).
- Adding and removing dependencies, which Gitea already supports.
- Merge queues, and rebasing dependent pull requests automatically.

## Open Questions
None

## Design Decisions
Added per commit during implementation, as in #53 and #54.

## Scope
medium (3 points). Touches the rule that decides whether a dependency is resolved, and the three ways a pull request gets merged (the merge button, the API and a scheduled merge) with their error messages; a small change in each, plus tests for every path.

## Scope Change Reasoning
Split from #20, which asked for this merge-order rule along with work Gitea already does: adding and removing dependencies, and blocking merges on open dependencies on the web, the API and scheduled merges. This issue takes the part that is missing, a pull request that was closed without merging.

> Blocked by #<A>, which decides which dependencies block a merge.

## User Story

As a maintainer about to merge a pull request, I want its page to tell me which dependencies still block it, and whether each one is open, merged or closed, so that I know why it cannot be merged before I press Merge, not after.

## User Scenario
Sam's pull request #12 depends on pull request #11, which was closed without merging, and on issue #9, which is still open. When a maintainer opens #12, the merge box, where blockers such as missing approvals already appear, says "This pull request is blocked by its dependencies:" followed by links to #11 and #9. No merge button is offered.

In the sidebar, the "Depends on" list shows each entry's state: #11 "Closed", #9 "Open". Today both just look closed or open, and a merged pull request looks the same as a closed one. Once #9 is closed and #11 is reopened and merged, the merge box shows the merge button again.

| Dependency | Sidebar shows | Blocks merging (#<A>) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open issue or pull request | Open | Yes |
| Closed issue | Closed | No |
| Merged pull request | Merged | No |
| Pull request closed without merging | Closed | Yes |

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a pull request with a dependency that blocks merging, when it is opened, then its merge box shows "This pull request is blocked by its dependencies:" followed by a link to each blocking dependency, with its number and title.
- [ ] AC2: Given the same, when a user with merge rights opens it, then no merge button is offered.
- [ ] AC3: Given a pull request with no dependencies, or whose dependencies are all resolved, when it is opened, then the merge box looks as it does today.
- [ ] AC4: Given a blocking dependency the viewer cannot read, when they open the pull request, then the merge box counts it as "You do not have permission to read 1 dependency" without its title, as the sidebar does today.
- [ ] AC5: Given the "Depends on" or "Blocks" list in the sidebar of an issue or pull request, when it is shown, then each entry shows its state: "Open", "Closed", or "Merged" for a merged pull request.
- [ ] AC6: Given a repository with "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" turned off, when a pull request is opened, then neither the merge box nor the sidebar shows dependencies, as the sidebar does today.

## Out of Scope
- Which dependencies block a merge, and refusing the merge: Issue (#<A>)
- Showing dependencies on the issue and pull request lists.
- Changing how dependencies are added or removed.

## Open Questions
None

## Design Decisions
Added per commit during implementation, as in #53 and #54.

## Scope
medium (3 points). Touches two parts of the pull request page, the merge box and the sidebar's dependency lists, plus one new message; moderate changes to the page's data and templates, with browser tests for both parts.

## Scope Change Reasoning
Split from #20, which asked for pull request pages to show prerequisites, their status, and links to dependent pull requests. The lists and links already exist in the sidebar; this issue adds the states and the blocker in the merge box.

## Observed Behavior
- On the web and through the API, a loop of three or more dependencies is accepted: #1 depends on #2, #2 on #3, and #3 on #1. Only a loop of two is refused ("You cannot create a dependency with two issues that block each other."). None of the issues in such a loop can be closed, and none of the pull requests can be merged, until someone removes a dependency.
- Through the API, an issue or pull request can be made to depend on itself, after which it can never be closed or merged. The web refuses this with "You cannot make an issue depend on itself."
- Through the API, adding a dependency that already exists, or one that makes a loop of two, answers 500 Internal Server Error instead of saying what is wrong.

## Expected Behavior
- A dependency that would make a loop of any length is refused. On the web the message is "You cannot add this dependency, because the issues would block each other in a loop."
- A self-dependency is refused through the API, as it is on the web.
- The API answers 422 Unprocessable Entity for a loop or a self-dependency, and 409 Conflict for a dependency that already exists, as the close-reason endpoint does for invalid and conflicting requests.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. In a repository with dependencies enabled, open issues #1, #2 and #3.
2. On #1, add #2 as a dependency; on #2, add #3; on #3, add #1. All three are accepted.
3. Try to close any of the three: each is refused because of its open dependency.
4. Through the API, `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/1/dependencies` with `{"owner": "{owner}", "repo": "{repo}", "index": 1}`. Issue #1 now depends on itself.
5. Send a request from step 4 a second time, with `"index": 2`: the API answers 500.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given #1 depends on #2 and #2 on #3, when a user adds #1 as a dependency of #3 on the web, then it is refused with "You cannot add this dependency, because the issues would block each other in a loop." and nothing is added.
- [ ] AC2: Given the same, or #1 depending on #2 alone, when the dependency that closes the loop is added through the API, then the API answers 422 Unprocessable Entity and nothing is added.
- [ ] AC3: Given an issue or pull request, when it is added as its own dependency through the API, then the API answers 422 Unprocessable Entity and nothing is added.
- [ ] AC4: Given #1 already depends on #2, when the same dependency is added through the API, then the API answers 409 Conflict.
- [ ] AC5: Given dependencies that do not make a loop, such as #1 and #2 both depending on #3, when they are added on the web or through the API, then they are accepted, as today.

## Additional Information
Found on `main` at `1410c7d404` while splitting #20. Once a pull request stays blocked until its dependencies are resolved (#<A>), a loop means none of its pull requests can ever be merged.

Evidence of the fix: each AC gets a test that fails on `main` and passes after the fix, listed in the PR's Test Evidence.

## Out of Scope
- Finding or removing loops that already exist.
- Which dependencies block closing or merging: Issue (#<A>)

## Design Decision
Added per commit during implementation, as in #53 and #54.

## Scope
small (2 points). Touches the check made when a dependency is added, and the API's answers to it; one rule widened from loops of two to loops of any length, plus three status codes and their tests.

## Scope Change Reasoning
Split from #20, which asked for self-dependencies and dependency cycles to be rejected. Gitea already rejects both on the web, but only loops of two, and the API skips the self-dependency check.

I've drafted three sub-issues for #20. The main thing to know first: **most of #20 is already in Gitea.** Pull requests can already depend on each other. The sidebar lists them under "Depends on" and "Blocks", and the web merge button, the API and scheduled merges all refuse to merge while a dependency is open (`services/pull/check.go:223`). The upstream issue #20 was based on (go-gitea/gitea#38231) was closed on Oct 8 for this reason.

Here's what's actually missing:

1. **A closed but unmerged pull request counts as done.** The check only looks at whether it's closed (`models/issues/dependency.go:190`). This is #20's core ask, and it isn't met today.
2. **API merge returns 500** when dependencies block it. Every other "can't merge" reason returns 405 (`routers/api/v1/repo/pull.go:970-987`).
3. **Turning dependencies off in settings doesn't stop them blocking merges.** They are hidden and can't be removed, but still block the merge. Closing an issue already ignores them when the setting is off (`models/issues/issue_update.go:71`).
4. **The merge box doesn't say why a merge is blocked.** You only find out after pressing Merge. In the sidebar, a merged pull request looks the same as a closed one.
5. **Loops of three or more are accepted**, because only two-issue loops are checked (`dependency.go:136`). The API also accepts self-dependencies and answers 500 for a dependency that already exists.

One trap is guarded in A's AC6: closing a pull request uses the same "no dependencies left" check as merging. A naive change would stop people closing B while A is closed but unmerged.

```markdown
## Summary
Let a pull request depend on other pull requests and issues, and keep it from merging until they are done, so that dependent changes never land before the code they need.

Gitea already does most of this:
- Adding and removing dependencies on pull requests and issues, on the web ("Depends on" and "Blocks" in the sidebar) and through the API.
- Refusing to merge a pull request while one of its dependencies is open, from the merge button, through the API, and for a scheduled merge.
- Refusing loops of two, and, on the web, self-dependencies.
- Turning dependencies on or off per repository with "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests".

## User Story
As a maintainer reviewing related changes, I want Gitea to block a dependent pull request until its prerequisites merge, so that unfinished dependencies do not break the target branch.

## Sub-issues
- #<A>: a pull request that was closed without merging keeps blocking the pull requests that depend on it, and every way of merging refuses with a clear error.
- #<B>: the pull request page shows which dependencies block it, and whether each one is open, merged or closed. Blocked by #<A>.
- #<C>: loops of any length, and self-dependencies through the API, are refused.

This issue is closed once all three are.

## Out of Scope
- A separate setting for merge blocking; the existing "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" setting decides.
- Changes to cross-repository dependencies, which Gitea already allows unless the site administrator turns them off.
- Merging a scheduled pull request the moment its last dependency merges.
- Automatic rebasing of dependent pull requests, and merge queues.

## Scope
large (8 points), split into #<A> (medium, 3 points), #<B> (medium, 3 points) and #<C> (small, 2 points). Together they touch the dependency rules, the three ways a pull request gets merged, the pull request page and the API's dependency endpoints; each sub-issue states its own scope.

## Scope Change Reasoning
The original version asked for adding and removing dependencies, showing them on the pull request page, rejecting self-dependencies and cycles, a setting for merge blocking, closed-but-unmerged prerequisites not counting, and the same rule on every merge path. Most of that already exists in Gitea, so the sub-issues cover only what is missing: a closed but unmerged pull request still counting as done (#<A>), the page not saying what blocks a merge (#<B>), and longer loops and API self-dependencies being accepted (#<C>). The separate setting was dropped in favour of the existing one.

## Source
Upstream [go-gitea/gitea#38231, Dependent pull requests](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/issues/38231). Upstream closed it on Oct 8, 2026 as already covered by [go-gitea/gitea#7901](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/7901). This proposal limits the first version to one repository.

## AI Disclosure
Used claude-code for the rewrite of this issue, followed by my changes and proofing.
